items.readable_text:
Content:
When we take a power of a trigonometric function, we write the power after the function but before the argument.

Content:
For instance [MATH: \sin^2 30^\circ] is the same as [MATH: (\sin30^\circ)^2.] Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: \sin^{2} 30^{∘}|= (\sin 30^{∘})^{2}; = ((1)/(2))^{2}; = (1)/(4).]

Content:
Similarly, [MATH: \tan^4 \left(\dfrac\pi 3\right)] is the same as [MATH: \left(\tan \left(\dfrac\pi 3\right)\right)^4.] Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: \tan^{4} ((π)/(3))|= (\tan ((π)/(3)))^{4}; = (sqrt(3))^{4}; = (sqrt(3))^{2} ⋅ (sqrt(3))^{2}; = 3 ⋅ 3; = 9.]

items.title: Evaluating an Expression Involving Special Angles in Degrees

key_prerequisites.name: Finding Trigonometric Ratios of Special Angles Using the Unit Circle

sections.normalized_html:
Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

  • Let's first consider the angle [MATH: 150^\circ.] From the unit circle, we see that the angle [MATH: 150^\circ] corresponds to the point [MATH: \left( -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2} \right).] Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the [MATH: y]-coordinate, we have [MATH: \sin 150^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}.]

  • Now, let's consider the angle [MATH: 240^\circ.] From the unit circle, we see that the angle [MATH: 240^\circ] corresponds to the point [MATH: \left( -\dfrac{1}{2}, -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right).] Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the [MATH: y]-coordinate, we have [MATH: \sin 240^\circ = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.]

Using the fact that [MATH: \csc{\theta} = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta},] we have

[MATH: \csc 240^{∘}|= (1)/(\sin 240^{∘}); = (1)/((− (sqrt(3))/(2))); = − (2)/(sqrt(3)).]

Finally, we combine the results:

[MATH: \sin^{2} (150^{∘}) + 2\csc^{2} (240^{∘})|= ((1)/(2))^{2} + 2(− (2)/(sqrt(3)))^{2}; = (1)/(4) + 2((4)/(3)); = (1)/(4) + (8)/(3); = (35)/(12)]

sections.normalized_html:
Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

  • Let's first consider the angle [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{6}.] From the unit circle, we see that the angle [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{6}] corresponds to the point [MATH: \left( \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2} \right).] Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the [MATH: x]-coordinate, we have [MATH: \cos\left( \dfrac {\pi} {6}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.]

  • Now, let's consider the angle [MATH: \dfrac \pi 4.] From the unit circle, we see that the angle [MATH: \dfrac \pi 4] corresponds to the point [MATH: \left( \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \right).] Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the [MATH: y]-coordinate, we have [MATH: \sin\left( \dfrac {\pi} {4}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.]

Finally, we combine the results:

[MATH: 4\cos^{2} ((π)/(6)) − \sin ((π)/(4))|= 4((sqrt(3))/(2))^{2} − (sqrt(2))/(2); = 3 − (sqrt(2))/(2)]

Item 2 — Example: Evaluating an Expression Involving Special Angles in Degrees

Example Prompt:
Evaluate [MATH: \sin^2\left(150^\circ\right) + 2\csc^2\left(240^\circ\right).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

[IMG: /graphics/820f6cdc6be9985b82e5417e40f07d3b]

- Let's first consider the angle [MATH: 150^\circ.] From the unit circle, we see that the angle [MATH: 150^\circ] corresponds to the point [MATH: \left( -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2} \right).] Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the [MATH: y]-coordinate, we have [MATH: \sin 150^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}.]
- Now, let's consider the angle [MATH: 240^\circ.] From the unit circle, we see that the angle [MATH: 240^\circ] corresponds to the point [MATH: \left( -\dfrac{1}{2}, -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right).] Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the [MATH: y]-coordinate, we have [MATH: \sin 240^\circ = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.]

Using the fact that [MATH: \csc{\theta} = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta},] we have

[MATH: \csc 240^{∘}|= (1)/(\sin 240^{∘}); = (1)/((− (sqrt(3))/(2))); = − (2)/(sqrt(3)).]

Finally, we combine the results:

[MATH: \sin^{2} (150^{∘}) + 2\csc^{2} (240^{∘})|= ((1)/(2))^{2} + 2(− (2)/(sqrt(3)))^{2}; = (1)/(4) + 2((4)/(3)); = (1)/(4) + (8)/(3); = (35)/(12)]
